# Stage 3 — Part 2: Dataset vs Feature Space, and Why More Observations Do Not Mean More Dimensions

We already have the structure

$$
X= \begin{bmatrix} 10&4\\ 12&5\\ 9&3\\ 11&5 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

At this point, a very common cognitive mistake appears naturally:

> “There are 4 rows and 2 columns. Does that mean the data is 4-dimensional, 2-dimensional, or somehow both?”

The answer depends on **what object we are talking about**. That is the exact place where we need to separate roles.

## 1. One observation has a certain number of descriptive slots

Take one row:

$$
x_1= \begin{bmatrix} 10\\ 4 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

This one observation is described using two feature values: $\text{length},\quad \text{width}.$ So this observation needs two numerical coordinates to specify its location in the chosen feature representation. That is why the feature space is two-dimensional. Not because there are two columns visually. The deeper reason is:

$$
\boxed{ \text{two independently addressable feature quantities are needed to describe one observation}. }
$$

The columns merely store those two quantities. So: $x_1\in\mathbb R^2.$ Read this semantically as:

> $`x_1`$ is represented using two real-valued feature coordinates.

## 2. Now add another observation

Take:

$$
x_2= \begin{bmatrix} 12\\ 5 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Does adding `x_2` create a third dimension? No. Why not? Because `x_2` is described using the same two kinds of quantities: $\text{length},\quad \text{width}.$ We did not invent a new feature. We merely observed another object under the same representation scheme. So both observations live in the same space: $x_1\in\mathbb R^2, \qquad x_2\in\mathbb R^2.$ Visually:

```text
width
  ↑
6 |
5 |                      • x₂=(12,5)
4 |                 • x₁=(10,4)
3 |
2 |
1 |
0 +--------------------------------→ length
```

Two observations are two **points** in one two-dimensional feature space. The number of points does not define the dimension of the space.

## 3. This is the distinction we need

The feature space answers:

> What numerical degrees of freedom are available to describe one observation?

The dataset answers:

> Which observations have we actually collected?

These are different questions. So:

$$
\boxed{ \text{feature space} \neq \text{dataset} }
$$

More explicitly:

$$
\boxed{ \text{feature space} = \text{set of possible feature representations} }
$$

while

$$
\boxed{ \text{dataset} = \text{finite collection of observed points in that space} }
$$

This is one of the most important distinctions before PCA.

## 4. A map analogy, but with exact roles

Imagine a city map. The map provides two positional dimensions: $\text{east-west},\quad \text{north-south}.$ Those define the coordinate space. Now suppose we mark 3 restaurants on the map. The map does not become 3-dimensional. Suppose we mark 100 restaurants. Still two-dimensional. Why? Because the number of marked locations changed. The coordinate system did not. That is the same distinction here. Our feature space: $(\text{length},\text{width})$ is analogous to the map's coordinate structure. Our observations are points placed into that structure. So:

$$
\boxed{ \text{more observations} \Rightarrow \text{more points} }
$$

not:

$$
\boxed{ \text{more observations} \Rightarrow \text{more dimensions} }
$$

## 5. Where does $`n\times d`$ come from?

Now suppose we use conventional notation: $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}.$ Do not read this yet as matrix dimensions only. Read the symbols by role: $n=\text{number of observations}$ $d=\text{number of features used to represent one observation}.$ So: $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ means:

> we collected `n` observations, and every observation is represented by `d` numerical feature values.

That is the semantics. The storage shape follows from that meaning. For our example: $n=4,\qquad d=2.$ Therefore: $X\in\mathbb R^{4\times2}.$ This does **not** mean each observation is four-dimensional. Each observation is still: $x_i\in\mathbb R^2.$ The `4` belongs to the **collection size**. The `2` belongs to the **representation size of each observation**. Programming analogy:

```text
X:
    collection of 4 observations

each observation:
    structure containing 2 feature values
```

So:

```text
dataset size = 4
observation representation size = 2
```

Those are different types of counts.

## 6. Why matrix shape can mislead us

The matrix:

$$
X= \begin{bmatrix} 10&4\\ 12&5\\ 9&3\\ 11&5 \end{bmatrix}
$$

has four rows. Purely syntactically, we can say: $\text{shape}(X)=(4,2).$ But syntax does not tell us ontology. The first axis means: $\text{which observation?}$ The second axis means: $\text{which feature?}$ So the indices in $X_{ij}$ have different semantic types: $i:\text{observation index}$ $j:\text{feature index}.$ Then: $X_{ij}$ means:

> the value of feature $`j`$ measured for observation $`i`$.

This is extremely important for mathematical programming. The two indices are both integers computationally. But semantically: $i\neq j$ in role. They index different kinds of things. That is analogous to programming where two values may both be `int` but one is a `user_id` and one is a `product_id`. Same low-level type. Different semantic role.

## 7. Why averaging along different axes asks different questions

Now this distinction begins to pay off. Suppose:

$$
X= \begin{bmatrix} 10&4\\ 12&5\\ 9&3\\ 11&5 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Take the first column:

$$
\begin{bmatrix} 10\\ 12\\ 9\\ 11 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

These are all values of the **same feature**: $\text{length}.$ So averaging them asks:

> What is the average length across observations?

That is semantically coherent:

$$
\bar{x}_{\text{length}} = \frac{10+12+9+11}{4} = 10.5.
$$

Now take the second column:

$$
\begin{bmatrix} 4\\ 5\\ 3\\ 5 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Average:

$$
\bar{x}_{\text{width}} = \frac{4+5+3+5}{4} = 4.25.
$$

So the dataset center in feature coordinates will eventually become:

$$
\mu= \begin{bmatrix} 10.5\\ 4.25 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

We are not beginning Stage 4 yet. But notice what made this operation meaningful:

> we aggregated across observations while preserving feature identity.

That is the semantic meaning of a column-wise mean.

## 8. Why averaging across a row is a different question

Take observation 1:

$$
x_1= \begin{bmatrix} 10\\ 4 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

If we compute:

$$
\frac{10+4}{2}=7,
$$

what does `7` mean? If both quantities happen to be centimeters, the units do not immediately expose a contradiction. But semantically we have combined: $\text{length}$ and $\text{width}.$ The result is not automatically a meaningful physical property. What question would `7` answer? Without some explicit modeling reason, there may be none. So:

$$
\boxed{ \text{numerically legal} \not\Rightarrow \text{semantically meaningful} }
$$

This is one of the deepest recurring lessons in your learning framework. NumPy will happily calculate either direction. Mathematics does not ask only:

> Can the machine perform this operation?

It asks:

> What relationship does this operation express?

## 9. Now consider three features

Suppose we add thickness: $[\text{length},\text{width},\text{thickness}].$ One observation becomes:

$$
x_1= \begin{bmatrix} 10\\ 4\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now the feature space is: $\mathbb R^3.$ Why? Because one observation requires three feature coordinates. If we then collect 1,000 observations: $X\in\mathbb R^{1000\times3}.$ The feature space remains three-dimensional. We simply have 1,000 points in it. So:

$$
\boxed{ d = \text{dimension of the chosen feature representation} }
$$

while:

$$
\boxed{ n = \text{number of samples drawn or collected within that representation}. }
$$

This distinction will later protect us from misunderstanding PCA.

## 10. A subtle point: feature dimension is chosen, not discovered yet

Suppose we choose: $[\text{length},\text{width},\text{thickness}].$ Then formally our observations live in a three-feature representation. But perhaps in the manufactured objects: $\text{thickness}=0.1\times\text{length}$ for every component. Then thickness carries no independent variation beyond length. We may still write three numbers per observation:

$$
x_i= \begin{bmatrix} \text{length}\\ \text{width}\\ \text{thickness} \end{bmatrix}.
$$

So the **representation has three feature coordinates**. But the observed data may occupy only a lower-dimensional structure inside that three-dimensional feature space. This is the distinction we glimpsed at the end of Stage 2. Example: $X\in\mathbb R^{1000\times3}$ does not guarantee the dataset genuinely varies in three independent ways. That later becomes a central PCA question:

> How many independently important directions of variation are actually present in these $`d`$ measured coordinates?

But we are not solving that yet. For now distinguish:

$$
\boxed{ \text{ambient feature dimension} }
$$

from:

$$
\boxed{ \text{structure actually occupied by the data}. }
$$

The first comes from our representation design. The second must be learned from the dataset. That separation is foundational for everything ahead.

## 11. Why a dataset is not itself “the space”

Suppose we only observe:

$$
x_1= \begin{bmatrix} 10\\ 4 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2= \begin{bmatrix} 12\\ 5 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Our dataset contains only two points. But the feature space includes possible observations we have never seen:

$$
\begin{bmatrix} 8\\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \begin{bmatrix} 15\\ 6 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \begin{bmatrix} 10.7\\ 4.9 \end{bmatrix},
$$

and infinitely many others. So:

$$
\boxed{ \text{dataset} \subset \text{feature space} }
$$

conceptually. The feature space defines what representations are possible. The dataset gives actual observed instances. This resembles programming:

```text
type/schema:
    defines allowed structure

instances:
    actual values that exist
```

Feature space is closer to the allowed state space. Dataset is the collection of realized states.

## 12. This prepares an important question: what structure do the observations collectively show?

Once we have many points in a shared feature space, we can stop asking only:

> What is observation $`i`$?

and begin asking:

> What do the observations collectively reveal?

That is a major change of scope. Before: $x_i$ our object of attention was one observation. Now: $X$ our object of attention becomes the dataset as a whole. This changes the kinds of questions available. For one observation, we can ask:

- what are its feature values?
- where is it located?

For the dataset, we can ask:

- where are observations concentrated?
- how much do they vary?
- which features vary together?
- are there recurring directions?
- does the dataset occupy all of feature space or mostly a smaller structure?

These are not properties of one $`x_i`$. They are **dataset-level properties**. This distinction will later separate:

$$
\boxed{ \text{observation-specific coordinate} }
$$

from:

$$
\boxed{ \text{dataset-wide learned structure}. }
$$

That distinction becomes critical in PCA and embeddings.

## 13. Stage 3 semantic audit

For $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d},$ **Object:** a dataset consisting of `n` observations. **Each row:** one observation. **Each column:** one selected feature measured across observations. **Reference/representation scheme:** the ordered set of `d` feature definitions, including their units and meanings. **Feature space:** the space of possible `d`-feature representations. **Dataset:** the particular `n` observed points. **Why is the feature space** **`d`****-dimensional?** Because each observation requires `d` feature coordinates under the chosen representation. **Why does adding rows not increase dimension?** Because adding observations adds more instances under the same representation scheme; it does not add new feature directions. **What information does** **`X`** **retain?** The selected feature values for the collected observations. **What does it discard?** Properties not measured, and objects never observed.

## 14. The key chain to retain

The whole Stage 3 structure now looks like:

$$
\boxed{ \text{real object} \rightarrow \text{selected features} \rightarrow \text{feature values} \rightarrow \text{observation vector }x_i }
$$

Then:

$$
\boxed{ \text{many observation vectors} \rightarrow \text{dataset }X }
$$

And separately:

$$
\boxed{ \text{chosen feature scheme} \rightarrow \text{feature space} }
$$

So:

$$
\boxed{ x_i=\text{one point in feature space} }
$$

while:

$$
\boxed{ X=\text{collection of observed points in that space}. }
$$

This distinction is now sufficient to move into Stage 4. The next problem is no longer “what is an observation?” It becomes:

> **Given many observations scattered through the same feature space, what should we use as a common reference point if we want to describe how each observation differs from the dataset as a whole?**

That need will naturally produce the **mean as a reference point**, and from there **centering** will emerge as a reference change rather than as the mechanical instruction “subtract the mean.”
